title: Share your setup, how did you start and what did you build thanks to AI?
author: Fair-Rip286
selftext:
I am exploring some game ideas and I found this amazing community, I am honestly not an AI-hater and I appreciate the ideas and the work more than come manual code writing. 

Considering the tools, I was thinking about using Unity and simple Steamworks libraries for small multiplayer lobbies, but I have 0 experience in game dev.

Ironically I am a programmer, but all I have ever built is either web based or C++ (a decade ago) and my job now unfortunately is php software for a small EU company. Literally all useless for game developing. 

So what setup would you suggest? Where is the most difficult or manual part and how do you use Claude? Like inside Unity or with a terminal?

I have seen people saying they one-shot Claude creating entire games but I am honestly confused on what setup they would have to be able to do everything with Claude.

comments.author: Cruxikus
comments.body:
I have right now 2 Claude Pro Accounts.
One will be switched to Chatgpt next month.

Plan while I walk, voice recording, get it transcribed by YouTube for free after upload set on privat. Have se free Ai agenda filter out the ramle.

That I feed into Claude Claude gives me prompt for code.

replies.author: Fair-Rip286
replies.body:
I was more curious about the exact developing setup, like the tools needed and what you do to check the code or run the game.

Cool ideas anyway!

replies.author: Cruxikus
replies.body:
I got the Claude desktop app and it works in the folder of my godot project.
You can run tests in just Godot no need for anything else.
Audacity is very helpful. Pyxeledit and Aesprite if needed.

Don't make it more complicated than it need to be

replies.author: Fair-Rip286
replies.body:
Why Godot and not more known (and so trained on) engines? Really just curious since I'm new to this.

Thanks for the tips! Do you also let Claude manage the "creative" part with UI, icons, or some 3D models and generally assets or do you load all separately?

I think having that managed by a human could be helpful in case of commercialization since generated assets could be hard to verify and defend.

replies.author: Cruxikus
replies.body:
Godot hast its mcp (I dont know if claude code rly does need it) is free. It's so light weight it starts right up with no real loading time and is open source no license fee ever and forever

Well at first I worked on guidelines and anti prompts.
Those were stuck in the project folder and are Codes holy Bible ist must work and life by.

But soon I wanted better looking art and took other more capable ai agents to help.

But general yes I let code do its thing. The I test it and let it keep adjusting.

Sometimes when you do not know how to fix values in the code you ask it to take the valves from a config you can edit like volume or something you don't want to lose tokes and fine-tuning the audio.

replies.author: StrategySilent9360
replies.body: What agents do you use for art?

replies.author: Cruxikus
replies.body:
Chatgpt generates what I feed into perchance.org/ai-pixel-art-generator.
Then I feed portraits back to Chatgpt so I will do party at campfire and stuff like that.

Pyxeledit is used to fix small mistakes

comments.author: Shalke97
comments.body: I use Claude for my programming and Codex As a Designer. I released a Steam Game with it. Grim Reach Idle

replies.author: Fair-Rip286
replies.body:
Can I ask what kind of prompting style you used for this specific icon type? I really like it, it's a good mix between realism and item-like.

Cool game overall! Congrats. 

https://preview.redd.it/mbxja9zv5dhh1.png?width=683&format=png&auto=webp&s=aa627032362510e7a2144713dfb919a45d8dfe4f

replies.author: Shalke97
replies.body: Glad you like it. I started with ChatGPT to get the style right on one item, i wanted it to fit into my semi-realism dark fantasy world. As soon as chatGPT got some right, i let him made some in bulk to have references for future generation. Now everytime i use it in the CLI, it will reference the assets and generates images with transparent alpha backgrounds easily. Just try "Dark Fantasy - Realistic gritty art style"

replies.author: Silver-Chipmunk7744
replies.body:
Nice congrats dude. Looks pretty neat.

Building an idle game with AI is tricky. I have been working on one and i never truly feel happy about it.

comments.body:

>what did you build thanks to AI?

Mainly prototypes. You can view a few on my profile

comments.author: That1guy4226
comments.body:
So, Early this year I swapped roles with my wife. I am now a stay at home dad after having been in very hands on, physical jobs for the past 25 years. Always loved games but never had the time or opportunity to learn. well my wife mentioned that ChatGPT could help you make games so I became curious. I started just over two months ago and have been absolutely amazed at what has been possible.   
  
I mostly use the codex desktop app, with the 5x pro plan. but cluade can be setup much the same way. if you setup proper guiderails and skills for your ai to use it can do really cool stuff. This is an entirely ai made game in godot. Its kinda like Worldbox but on a functioning globe.  
  
I know that there is a lot that I dont know but I am learning so much as I continue pursuing this path

comments.author: aeronauts-dev
comments.body: I'm two weeks into building a multiplayer game in Unreal engine with CC. I think the key thing is to break up the game into smaller pieces that Claude can build & test in isolation. So far I have 3 main components  - the UE project which has everything, the 'simulator' app which is written in Rust and it just implements the game logic with no graphics, and the GUI rendering system. Both the simulator and the GUI can be run and tested in isolation. Claude is much faster and more successful when it can 'see' and work on smaller parts like that, compared running and testing the entire Unreal game every time it does anything.

replies.author: kryptondog
replies.body: Agreed that siloing off portions of the project seems to be a great help - I’m building a sprite based dungeon crawler, and I eventually split off the sprite editor (which is shaping up to be a cool project in its own right) from the game. Seems to stop drift and Opus 5’s tendency to sometimes second guess itself needlessly.
